questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Distributive Law
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the distributive law on the right:

$$
AC-BC=(A-B)C.
$$

So, compute $A-B$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-B & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4{I}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}AC-BC & =(A-B)C \\  & =(4{I}_{3})C \\  & =4C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3\times 3$ matrix, which will require finding $9$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $2\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding $2$ entries.

So, we find the product $BC$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $A$ by $BC:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =A(BC) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 15 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication
questions.problem:
Given that $A$ and $B$  are $4\times 4$ matrices,  and ${I}_{4}$ is the $4\times 4$ identity matrix,  which of the following statements are always true?

- $AB=BA$
- $A{I}_{4}={I}_{4}A$
- $A(B+{I}_{4})=AB+A$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $AB\ne BA$ in general.

- Statement II is true. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, however, multiplication by the identity matrix is always commutative. In this case, we have  $A{I}_{4}={I}_{4}A=A.$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+{I}_{4})=AB+A{I}_{4}=AB+A$ in general.

Therefore, only statements II  and III are true.

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC = (AB)C = A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3 \times 1$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3 \times 3$ matrix that will require finding $9$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3 \times 1$ matrix that will require finding only $3$ entries.

So, we find the product $BC$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $A$ by $BC\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =A(BC) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

- $A(B+C) = BA+CA$

- $A(B+C) = AB+AC$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+C) = AB + AC$ in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have

$$
AB + AC  \neq BA + CA.
$$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+B)C = AC+BC,$ and $A(B+C) = AB+AC$ in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.
